title: Lots of Careful and Care-Free Quizzing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart addresses a school leader’s observation that, following a PD session on the research benefits of frequent quizzing, teachers had implemented all quizzes on Fridays—creating test fatigue and stressful Thursday-night cramming. Stuart identifies the core misapplication: the retrieval practice research supports quizzing as a normal, embedded, low-pressure learning activity, not study-guide-style testing with advance notice and heavy grade consequences. In his own classroom, quizzes function as the study activity itself, carry classwork-level grade weight within a large point pool, and require no advance preparation by students. The distinction between quizzing for learning and quizzing for measurement is the corrective the article offers, with two clear takeaways: quiz frequently, but structure those quizzes so they carry minimal grade stakes and require no separate study behavior.
points: The retrieval practice research case for quizzing applies to informal, embedded, no-advance-notice quizzes that function as the studying itself—not to study-guide-backed, grade-consequential tests that require separate preparation.

Stuart’s classroom quizzes count as classwork within a large point category, so no individual quiz result significantly affects overall grade; this structural choice removes the high-stakes anxiety that transforms learning quizzes into testing events.
Students must be explicitly told that quizzing is a form of studying—not a measurement of readiness to be studied for—otherwise they import their own culturally formed ideas about what a test means.

The misapplication of quizzing research is predictable: teachers map their existing concept of ‘test’ onto the recommendation and produce the opposite of what the research supports—a concentrated, high-stakes event rather than a distributed, low-stakes habit.
quotes: low-stakes quizzes are a go-to lesson move in whatever courses I teach.
the leader is right — this IS a problem! The kind of effective testing that Benjamin Keep is speaking to isn’t the study guide kind; it’s the “quizzing is just a normal part of what we do” kind.
Students don’t have time or resources to “study” for these quizzes; the quizzes ARE THEIR OWN FORM of studying.

the core misunderstanding that some teachers took away from my session was that they were mapping their own ideas of what a test is — study guides, students given a warning about the test and pressure to study for it — versus the FOR LEARNING nature of tests that Dr. Keep is referencing from the research on retrieval practice.
you do need to be careful about how you present these quizzes and the degree to which they affect a student’s overall grade.
